observation.visible_scene: A wide, pale ground (snow- or ash-covered clearing) lies in front of a dense stand of tall, dark pine trunks under an overcast sky. A vertical column of white smoke rises from a fixed spot on the ground near the center of the frame and drifts toward the right. The forest, the ground texture, and the smoke source location stay put across the whole excerpt; the camera appears stationary (no background shift).
visible_changes: White smoke is already rising from the ground point in the first frame (an ongoing emission, not its onset) and continues throughout, slowly gaining height/opacity while drifting rightward from the same source.
From frame 1 to frame 36 the scene is essentially static except for the slow growth and rightward drift of the smoke plume; no camera motion is evident.
At frame 37 a small pink/red glow appears at the base of the smoke column on the ground, intensifying slightly by frame 38.
At frame 39 a bright white flash/burst erupts at that ground point, accompanied by lens-flare streaks, while the upper smoke column remains.

At frames 40-41 the bright flash collapses into a low, expanding white cloud of smoke/debris around the source, with dark fragments visible within and beside the cloud; the original smoke plume above still persists.
The explosion cloud expands outward from the source (deformation/expansion) rather than translating across the frame; the source point itself does not move.
outside_clip_unknowns: The cause of the steady smoke emission and of the flash/burst is not shown; no operator, ignition device, or prior impact is visible.
Whether the dark fragments are thrown debris or just shadowed smoke clumps, and what happens to the cloud after the last frame, are not captured.
The full start of the smoke plume and the final dissipation of the burst cloud lie outside the cropped segment.
uncertain_details: The rightward drift of the smoke could be wind or natural plume expansion; the excerpt does not distinguish them.
The exact identity of the bright burst (detonation, ignition, or flare) cannot be confirmed from the frames alone.
Minor apparent changes in smoke shape between adjacent frames may be rendering/interpolation artifacts rather than discrete physical events.
